fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Comedy as a vehicle for hard truths", "body": "Alex explains that he created the Flat Earth Man, a Texan cowboy voice, so he could sing about NASA and what he calls the globe deception while letting family and friends dismiss it as satire. His album covers the moon landing, the International Space Station and satellites, and he argues the comedic songs travel furthest because critical thinkers catch the deeper layer. He says fear is where the controllers want people and he refuses to live there, while Chance adds that humor and laughter never fail to dispel darkness, even alongside the fired up, serious approach."}, {"title": "From ringtones to internet folk hero", "body": "Alex traces his path from singing what he calls tepid love songs in bars to running a ringtone business from a converted garage in Essex, which he says is still his bread and butter. A visitor showed him a 9/11 video, which led to years of research into bloodline families, Alex Jones and David Icke, and then in 2016 the flat earth idea hit him. He released his first song in 2017, now lives in Spain, and values the freedom of not being signed to a major label. He also teases his friend David Weiss and praises Weiss's flat earth app."}, {"title": "True Solfeggio and the 432 versus 440 debate", "body": "Alex describes getting into the 432 versus 440 Hz conspiracy, calling 440 the fluoride of the music industry, and embedding tones into his guitar instrumental album True Solfeggio as what he calls an experiment. He says he was moved to tears while recording and keeps a folder of listener feedback. He argues that the popular 528 Hz tone has no relationship to 432 tuning, since middle C only reaches 528 when A is tuned to 444, and that in 432 tuning middle C becomes 512 Hz, which he calls the heart frequency."}, {"title": "Chance's 369 reading of the solfeggio tones", "body": "Chance presents an infographic from his tuning fork work, saying he does not buy claims like 528 for DNA repair but finds the standard tones, from 174 to 963, generate 3, 6 and 9 whichever way they are added or subtracted. He groups them in columns of one, four and seven, two, five and eight, and three, six and nine, reading them as oneness, generation and birth, and unpacks the word solfeggio as sol, fe, egg and io. Alex counters that the second itself is a man-made construct, and the two land on coherence and intent as what matters."}, {"title": "Division, fracture and speaking up", "body": "Chance suggests nature does addition, subtraction and multiplication but not division, and Alex argues that moving a keyboard from 432 to 440 fractures its whole number ratios. Both tie this to divide and conquer, from Pepsi versus Coke to the infighting Alex avoids in flat earth channels that trade insults and endless debates about gravity. Asked for advice to artists, Alex says truth music rarely pays but has made him happier than ever, and urges anyone to turn what they learn into something creative, while Chance links unexpressed truth to a blocked throat chakra."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Alex Michael is the Conspiracy Music Guru, aka "Flat Earth Man." His comedic delivery of conspiratorial gnosis via music has spread like wildfire, and in this chat we get to know his story, strategies for spreading truth in the age of censorship, thoughts on solfeggio frequencies, and the 440hz deception.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension, we we go deeper into how creative language can sneak past the A-Eye of Sauron, the inversions of the elites and actors, finding spirituality via conspiracy research, his new book series, cleaning up the gut, and more!

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Ether, consciousness and the magic of technology", "body": "Reconnecting after a dropped line, Chance Garton and Alex Michael turn a joke about digital daemons into a serious look at ether. Chance Garton holds that energy and consciousness are the same thing, so closed circuits of energy like computers must touch consciousness in some way. Alex Michael calls instant long distance conversation a kind of magic people have grown numb to. Chance Garton suggests external technology may be an outward echo of an innate human capacity for connection, while Alex Michael speculates that older cultures, including the so called Tartarian builders, once worked with the ether directly."}, {"title": "Creative ways around platform censorship", "body": "Alex Michael describes receiving YouTube strikes, including one for his heavy metal Big Pharma video, which was sung from the industry's own point of view and paired with imagery that was flagged as distressing. He explains why he stays on YouTube to reach a mainstream audience and why sarcasm, satire and memes help him get ideas across. Chance Garton adds that symbolic, cerebral framing and creative wordplay let creators carry meaning that filters struggle to catch. Both see human creativity as something automated moderation can never fully contain, though Alex Michael wonders whether his long term home may be his own website."}, {"title": "Conspiracy research as a road to spirituality", "body": "Chance Garton asks whether conspiracy research leads to spirituality, and Alex Michael agrees completely. He traces his own path from questioning the official 9/11 account to seeing the world as a spiritual contest between light and dark, and later to his belief that this is a created realm. That conviction, he says, left him feeling accountable to a Creator and committed to treating people better, themes he now writes into his songs. Chance Garton notes the path can also run the other way, since an honest spiritual seeker eventually notices inversion in the world, and he describes the two roads meeting in the middle."}, {"title": "Health as the root of creative energy", "body": "Chance Garton shares his experience that the healthier his body becomes, the more coherent his creative work grows and the more his imagination opens up. Alex Michael says his own research pushed him toward distilled water, home grown food and a small homestead, and he credits that shift with a burst of productivity and a sense of feeling younger. The pair also discuss gut health, fasting and cleansing as they personally see them, and Chance Garton links the root and sacral chakras to feelings of security and self worth. These are the speakers' own views rather than established medical guidance."}, {"title": "From satirical music videos to children's books", "body": "Alex Michael explains how his comedic music videos questioning NASA, the moon landings and mainstream cosmology found an unexpected audience in parents who used them to teach their children. At David Weiss's suggestion, he turned screenshots from those videos into colorful children's books meant to spark critical thinking, with four released and more planned. Chance Garton describes his own long distance sight observations and the warmth he felt among people with very different views at a Flat Earth gathering. Alex Michael closes by sharing his openness to a larger realm beyond Antarctica, which he frames as personal speculation."}]
